nodes.label: Programs that do tasks we call intelligent
nodes.whatItIs: AI is a large family of computer programs. All of them are strict computers doing exact arithmetic. They differ in where their behaviour comes from: written by a person, learned from examples, or learned from reward.

nodes.label: Written by a person
nodes.whatItIs: A person works out the behaviour and writes it down. The program does not change itself from data.

nodes.label: Learned from examples
nodes.whatItIs: The program is shown many examples. It adjusts itself until it does well on them, then is used on new cases.

nodes.label: Learned from reward
nodes.whatItIs: The program tries actions and gets a reward or a penalty. Over many tries it learns which actions pay off.

nodes.label: Rules
nodes.whatItIs: An expert system. A person writes if-then rules, and the program applies them to the facts it is given.
nodes.goodAt: Clear, checkable reasoning. You can see which rules led to an answer.
nodes.badAt: Anything the rule writers did not think of. Rules are slow to write, and hard to keep right as they pile up.
nodes.example: MYCIN, built in the 1970s, used hundreds of rules to suggest antibiotics for serious blood infections. It was a research system, not used routinely in hospitals.

nodes.label: Search
nodes.whatItIs: The program looks ahead through possible moves, scores where each one leads, and picks the move that leads to the best score.
nodes.goodAt: Games and puzzles with clear rules, where looking ahead pays off.
nodes.badAt: Problems with too many possibilities to look through, or with no clear way to score a position.
nodes.example: Chess programs look ahead through many possible moves before choosing one.

nodes.label: Classic machine learning
nodes.whatItIs: Simple models, such as decision trees and nearest-neighbour rules, that learn from a table of examples.
nodes.goodAt: Small, tidy data sets. Their answers are often easy to explain.
nodes.badAt: Raw images, sound and free text, unless a person first turns them into useful numbers.
nodes.example: Spam filters and credit scoring have long used models of this kind.

nodes.label: Neural networks
nodes.whatItIs: Many small units joined by adjustable numbers called weights. Training changes the weights to cut the errors on the examples.
nodes.goodAt: Patterns in images, sound and text, where it is hard to write rules by hand.
nodes.badAt: They usually need a lot of examples and computing. It is hard to see why they give an answer.
nodes.example: Recognising handwritten digits and recognising speech are well-known uses.

nodes.label: Q-learning
nodes.whatItIs: The program keeps a score for each action in each situation. It updates the scores from the rewards it receives.
nodes.goodAt: Learning a task by trial and error, when there is a clear reward and many tries are cheap.
nodes.badAt: Slow when there are many situations or the reward comes late. Trying things in the real world can be costly or unsafe.
nodes.example: Learning by reward in general (Q-learning is one method of it) has trained programs to play video games and board games.

nodes.label: Image networks
nodes.whatItIs: Neural networks that slide small filters over an image to find edges, then shapes, then whole objects.
nodes.goodAt: Telling what is in a picture, such as which digit was written.
nodes.badAt: They can fail on pictures unlike the ones they were trained on.
nodes.example: Reading handwritten digits, as on bank cheques and postal codes.

nodes.label: Memory networks
nodes.whatItIs: Neural networks that read a sequence one step at a time and carry a small memory from step to step.
nodes.goodAt: Short sequences, where what came just before matters.
nodes.badAt: The memory is small and fades, so they lose track of things from far back.
nodes.example: Before transformers, networks of this kind (recurrent networks, especially the LSTM kind) were widely used in speech recognition and machine translation.

nodes.label: Transformer
nodes.whatItIs: A neural network in which each piece of a text looks at other pieces, using attention. In GPT-style models, like the one in this app, each piece looks back only at the pieces before it. It is the kind inside most large language models.
nodes.goodAt: Long text, and learning from huge amounts of it. It handles many pieces at once.
nodes.badAt: The cost grows quickly as the text gets longer. It can give fluent answers that are wrong.
nodes.example: Large language models, which are built from transformers. The model in this app is a tiny one.

nodes.label: Diffusion
nodes.whatItIs: A neural network trained to remove a little noise from data. To make something new, it starts from pure noise and removes noise step by step.
nodes.goodAt: Making new images that look like the ones it was trained on.
nodes.badAt: It needs many steps for each result, so it is slow. It can make details that look right but are wrong.
nodes.example: Image generators such as Stable Diffusion work this way.
